lesson.title: Losing Electrons: How Atoms Become Positively Charged
lesson.summary: Cation formation is the process by which atoms lose one or more electrons to become positively charged ions, a step that requires an energy investment but sets up the electrostatic attraction at the heart of every ionic bond.
lesson.body:
A cation is an atom, or a group of atoms, that has lost one or more electrons and therefore carries an overall positive charge. Forming a cation is never free. Pulling a negatively charged electron away from a positively charged nucleus takes energy, and the amount of energy required is precisely what ionization energy measures. The first ionization energy of an atom is the energy needed to remove its outermost, most loosely held electron while the atom is in the gas phase. Elements with low ionization energies give up electrons easily and are the elements that most readily form cations, which is exactly why metals, especially those in groups 1 and 2, dominate the list of common cation-forming elements.

Sodium is the textbook case. Its first ionization energy is only about 496 kilojoules per mole, low because its single 3s electron is shielded from the nucleus by a full inner shell of core electrons and sits relatively far away. Removing that one electron leaves sodium with the electron configuration of neon, a filled, highly stable shell, so Na+ is what actually forms, with the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6. Removing a second electron from Na+ would mean tearing into that stable, complete shell, which takes vastly more energy, so sodium essentially never forms Na2+ under normal chemical conditions.

Magnesium extends the pattern one step further. Its first ionization energy, about 738 kilojoules per mole, removes one 3s electron to form Mg+. Its second ionization energy, about 1451 kilojoules per mole, is noticeably higher but still chemically accessible, removing the second 3s electron and leaving Mg2+ with the same stable neon configuration as Na+. A third ionization step would again require breaking into a complete inner shell, so magnesium reliably stops at a 2+ charge. This same logic explains why aluminum, one more step to the right, commonly forms Al3+ and essentially never goes further.

These patterns connect directly to the periodic trends in ionization energy. Ionization energy generally increases moving left to right across a period, as increasing nuclear charge pulls valence electrons in more tightly, and it generally decreases moving down a group, as each added electron shell puts the outermost electrons farther from the nucleus and shields them more effectively. That is why cation formation is easiest, and most common, toward the lower left of the periodic table, among the alkali and alkaline earth metals, and becomes progressively harder moving toward the upper right, where nonmetals hold onto their electrons tightly instead.

Once a cation has formed, it does not exist in isolation for long. The whole reason atoms bother paying the ionization energy cost is that the resulting cation can then form an ionic bond with a nearby anion, and the strong electrostatic attraction released by that bond, along with the enormous lattice energy released when countless such ion pairs pack into a crystal, more than repays the initial energy investment. Sodium's willingness to become Na+ is only the first half of the story that ends with a stable crystal of table salt.
